utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

The following day -- oh, and I'm open to any corrections from any Defence counsel if I've misidentified anybody. The following day in Banja Luka a parade of the Banja Luka special police was held. This unit had been established by Stojan Zupljanin in April. He'd actually requested armaments and other material from General Kukanjac of the JNA 2nd Military District which covered this area. He was apparently given them. And, in fact, as we will see from documents, possibly not from this opening, so as not to be too long, Stojan Zupljanin actually incorporated into the Banja Luka special police members of the SOS group that had, "invaded" Banja Luka the previous month. The parade was attended by Mico Stanisic, and it's this unit which came under the command in particular of a man called Ljuban Ecim, which was to commit some of the more serious crimes within the ARK. And we're going to show you a short clip of that parade, noting the armaments that were available to the Banja Luka special police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It also included units or police officers who came up from other substations. Helicopters. And then, as you can see, the blue uniforms. Sorry, we're speeding it up slightly so that -- just to give you some idea of the numbers of men and equipment available. Perhaps not terribly well-disciplined, judging by the waving to people in the crowd. And the police vehicles. So what we saw there were tanks, APCs, helicopters, men, and arms. I think that will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, I think you announced that we would see the accused Stanisic at the last video or maybe I misunderstood you, but my question goes actually to both videos. Have we seen Mr. Stanisic in any of the two videos that you have shown to us this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, no, you don't see him in this video. I don't think there is any disagreement though, however, he was there taking the parade, he wasn't actually marching in it, but you just don't happen to see him, and, no, he didn't -- he's not in the 12th of May video. And indeed, when he was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, he denied that he had attended the Assembly of the 12th of May, and at present we have no evidence to contradict that from documents or video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. So -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he is -- and as I say - and I'm sure if there is a dispute Mr. Zecevic will let me know - he was present at the parade which took place the day of the 12th of May. Before I move on to the crimes themselves, a brief outline, can I say one or two things about the sources of evidence that Your Honours will hear in this case. Witness evidence comes from the victims of the crimes, first of all, but the vast majority have testified in earlier trials. And accordingly, the Trial Chamber will have very limited opportunity to hear from them. Indeed, many will not be heard from at all in the sense that their evidence simply becomes part of the record through the procedures under Rule 92 bis. Of course the effect is that this tends to shift the emphasis of a trial as the concentration of the evidence that you will hear is on the actions by the accused and their subordinates. And it may appear that the suffering of the victims has been ignored. And simply, we want to say this because we know but the general public may not know that a trial such as this must always be a balancing exercise between the length of a trial and the right of a victim to be heard. And we've no doubt at all that each member of the Trial Chamber will read the evidence and that what happened to the victims will not be forgotten even though this doesn't, as I say, from public perception always seem apparent. Other witness testimony will come from the witnesses to the crimes, who were themselves not a party to those crimes or, indeed, a party to any criminal enterprise, and this includes internationals who were present for some of the events. You will also hear witness evidence from participants in the criminal enterprise. And can I say something about that. Those who fall into the category of participants, who worked in either the MUP or the VRS or the organs of government at either republican or municipal level are necessary for Your Honours to have a proper picture of the events in this case. But they do come - and I say this straight away with a health warning - in many cases they will be reluctant witnesses. They may well have their own agenda for testifying, reasons perhaps to minimise their own involvement or that of others. And it may be - and this is a matter entirely for Your Honours - that you come to the conclusion they are truthful about some matters but not about others. But that of course is a matter for Your Honours to assess, having listened to their evidence. And finally, of course, the evidence will come from documents and from experts in the political and military and police aspects of the case and those who have conducted an analysis of the -- the effects of this criminal enterprise, that is to say if it's not a creed, exhumations, and dispersal of the population. So can I turn now straight away to the actual crimes in the municipalities and the participation by the RS MUP. Three days after the 12th of May Assembly, Mico Stanisic issued an order that members of the MUP should be organised into war units. 15th of May, order: "1. Pursuant to the decision of the competent organs ... of the Serbian Republic ..." declaring an imminent threat of war we looked at yesterday. Also, "all authorised officials of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbian Republic ... shall be organised in war units (squads, platoons, companies, battalions, et cetera for the purposes of defending the territory of the Serbian republic. And all we need to look at on the rest of this is the signature and stamp of Mico Stanisic at the bottom. It will be a feature of this case that the police, the MUP -- members of the MUP were divided. Those who -- in the towns or the villages keeping order, carrying out -- or should be carrying out their police duties as we understand them, and those who were actually engaged in fighting together with the VRS. When they were engaged in fighting, they came under the command of the military. Otherwise, when dealing with, as I say, what we consider to be normal police procedures they stayed completely within the command of and the orders of the minister of the interior and his subordinates. On the same day, that is to say the 16th of May, Mico Stanisic appointed all his chiefs of the CSBs and he appointed Milenko Karisik as chief of what was called the police detachment, the special police unit -- I'm sorry, it was on the 15th of May. And then on the 16th of May he ordered his chiefs to provide daily reports, and the day after that -- as I say, there was a constant stream of orders coming from Mico Stanisic, he was demanding to know whether an order he had issued on the 15th of May had actually been complied with. So it wasn't just that he was issuing orders. He was actually also reminding them that they had to comply. And if we very quickly look at those documents, 16th of May he is sending an order to the security services centre, to the chief personally, and he says here: "In view of the tasks resulting from the order by the minister of the interior ... of the 15th of May ... for the purpose of monitoring combat operations and regular activities of the organs of the interior and in order to collect documentation on the crimes against the Serbian population ..." And again, that's a theme we will see later. The order to investigate - I shall be dealing with it at the very end of what I want to say - was always to investigate crimes committed against Serbs and later on war crimes committed against Serbs, very rarely to investigate crimes generally of the population. And the report goes on: " ... fax reports must be submitted daily to the Ministry of the Interior of Republic [indiscernible] ..." And then the rest of the document shows what the report had to contain. And if we go just quickly to IV -- sorry, back again. There we have it: "War crimes." Roman numeral IV, sorry. It again -- "These activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs." Then we go to the next document. 17th of May, first paragraph: "Send us reports on the measures taken on the order of the minister number strictly confidential" it gives the number, "of the 15th of May ..." So he doesn't wait two days before sending out a reminder. The seizure of power by the Bosnian Serb leaders in the municipalities that they had targeted to form part of their state, particularly those in the municipalities where the Serbs did not form a majority, in other words, Variant B, followed a similar pattern. And indeed, all these matters which I am about to refer to have been litigated so often that again they are all part of the adjudicated facts. The Serb population, as I mentioned yesterday, was clandestinely calmed and Serb Municipal Assemblies and Crisis Staffs were established. Propaganda was disseminated to make the Serb populace believe that atrocities would be committed against them by non-Serbs. And we've just picked one example. There are many. This was published -- it's called the Informator of the Serbian Democratic Party of Sanski Most. And if you go -- if we go, rather -- I go, you don't -- to the third page it starts: "Dear brother Serbs. "Do you know what our blood-thirsty enemies have been scheming for us? "What they had in mind was to gouge out our eyes, carve us up, hack our bodies to pieces, rape women and girls in front of their dearest, to circumcise, to destroy our religion, to crush us just because we happen to be Serbs. "Don't think anybody's family would have been spared. They had monsters ready and committing to raping Serbian women, and they had developed a system of killing each and every Serb. "Soon we will show everyone their horrible weapons, the Serb-cutters, swords from the middle ages, sledge-hammers, special knives, instruments to gouge out our eyes with, and instruments to carve us up. "A decent man shutters with horror ..." And then they give allegedly an example. Now, to us in the clinical atmosphere of this courtroom it may seem utterly incredible that anybody could believe such total and utter rubbish, but, of course, you're dealing with a population, a rural population for a large part, that was perhaps not quite as sophisticated and was all too ready to believe that this was true. And many of the internationals who were working there, particularly those who were -- had been sent there by the economic -- by the European Community as monitors noted how much the propaganda was being spread and how rumours became fact very, very quickly. Check-points were established manned by Bosnian Serb soldiers, by the MUP, and by so-called paramilitary formations, which was sometimes local Serbs, sometimes people that come from other parts of Bosnia or, indeed, from Serbia, the most famous perhaps being Captain Dragan's men or Arkan's men, the White Eagles, the Wolfs of Vucjak. The importance of the MUP in this plan may be seen by the fact that the assumption of power in the municipalities normally began with the take-over of the SJBs, then the administering of the loyalty oath, and then the dismissal of non-Serb members. Orders for disarmament were issued by the municipal Bosnian Serb or SDS Crisis Staff, and thereafter, depending on the nature of the municipality, the level of violence increased. Non-Serb villages and parts of towns were attacked by the combined forces of the military, the MUP, and again paramilitaries. And the attacks often began with the shelling of the area or village followed by the arrival of armed men in uniform. Those not killed in the attacks or when the forces came in were rounded up, men, women, and children. Unarmed men were summarily executed, some on the spot, some were taken elsewhere. Those who survived were taken to makeshift detention facilities. These included a disused open-cast mine, industrial complexes, football fields, schools, as well as police stations and actual prisons. And the police provided the guards for most or for many, if not all, of these facilities. The conditions therein were generally appalling. Overcrowding, lack of food, lack of water, lack of sanitary facilities, medical attention, if it was there, was limited. All of this was standard. Beatings of inmates by guards and those who were allowed into the detention facility were routine. Some of those beatings were severe enough to cause death. And women who were kept in these facilities, at least in some of them, were raped. Mass killings took place during transport to or from the facilities, and on at least one occasion, if not more, in the facility itself in Keraterm camp in Prijedor the inmates of room 44 -- 4 -- come back to that in a minute -- were all machine-gunned and killed. Looting and destruction of property almost invariably followed on attacks. Religious and cultural destruction took place throughout this period, not confined, in fact, to places where attacks had taken place, but even in places like Banja Luka which was so Serb-controlled that didn't happen. Mosques were blown up. In places where this degree of force was not needed for the Bosnian Serbs to seize power, for example, in Banja Luka, the non-Serbs lost their jobs and were subjected to a range of discriminatory measures which were perhaps the most extreme exemplified in a document that was issued by the Celinac Crisis Staff. Celinac was next door to Banja Luka. It was -- and there are other not dissimilar examples in this case. It's dated the 23rd of July, and it's a decision on the status of the non-Serbian population of the Celinac municipality. Article 1: "The execution of combat operations on the territory of Celinac municipality and further afield has given rise to basic reasons for giving the non-Serbian population of Celinac municipality a special status, with clearly expressed rights, obligations, and responsibilities." George Orwell would have been proud of that particular statement, a special status with expressed rights, obligations, and responsibilities. You will see that it names all the people, all of whom were, as you can see from the names, are of Muslim ethnicity. They were -- if you look at the next page. " ... considered as persons who previously acted negatively and compromised themselves in various ways, thereby harming the Serbian people, on account of which they are given a different status from other non-Serbian inhabitants." They have the right to live unhindered to health care, however -- and they will be permitted to leave the territory on the condition that their departure is conducted in an organised fashion. Article 5: "Until further notice, the citizens from Article 1 shall be: "Forbidden from moving around ... between 1600 and 0600 hours. "Forbidden from lingering in the street ... "Forbidden from bathing in the rivers ... "Forbidden from travelling without permission ... "Forbidden from owning any kind of fire-arm ..." Well, that was a bit unnecessary because by then all non-Serbs were -- actually been disarmed. "Forbidden from moving or using cars. " ... gathering in groups with more than three men ..." Et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And then in Article 6: "To turn out in an orderly fashion for work considered by the -- for tasks encompassed by work obligation." When the populations, non-Serb populations, were driven to leave, they were forced to sign a document which stated that they were voluntarily signing over their property to the Bosnian Serb state. When they left in buses or trains they were robbed of their valuables before or during transit. And in the end, as planned, either voluntarily or forcibly, hundreds of thousands of non-Serbs left the territory of the Republika Srpska. That's the general picture. What we would like to do now is just concentrate on one particular municipality for a little while just to show it in a little more detail what actually happened, and that municipality is Kotor Varos. In the 1991 census, the population of Kotor Varos was shown to be nearly 37.000 Serb, 38.1 per cent. 30 per cent were Muslim, and 29 per cent Croats. So a slight majority there of Serbs, but not enough. And the split was reflected in the 1990 elections, with the SDS receiving the highest number of votes, but they didn't get a pure majority. So they could be out-voted if the HDZ, the Croat party; and the SDA, the Muslims, banded together. And you can see now a map of Kotor Varos came within the area of Krajina. And photographs there of various places that you're going to hear about. The sawmill, the Catholic church, the SJB building, the medical centre, and the prison. And if we look at a map which shows the breakdown of -- can we make it a bit larger? Is that possible? Yeah. What we've got here is the various villages and what the -- the majority of the inhabitants were. So you've got Serbs in purple, green for Muslim, and Croats in red. And if we -- you see Kotor Varos and the town there. Here about Hanifici, Dabovci in particular, and other places. And Maslovare, I believe, I believe, and again I'm open to contradiction, is where Stojan Zupljanin was born. But certainly he was a native of Kotor Varos and a relative of his, Slobodan Zupljanin, was a captain in the JNA unit, the 122nd Infantry Brigade which covered the area and was to play a part in the events and who you will see in a video which we will show in a moment. Ante Mandic, who was president of the HDZ party in Kotor Varos, became president of the Assembly of the elections; Nedjelko Djekanovic, who was president of the SDS in Kotor Varos, became president of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly. The SDS party in Kotor Varos was a party to the founding of the community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities, which I spoke about yesterday. I'm interrupting myself again. It was pointed out to me yesterday that I had used a lot of acronyms during the course of my opening. Can I say there is a full list of most of the major acronyms attached to the pre-trial brief and also in the various expert reports. So that if you lost me yesterday, as you probably did, there is recourse to paper. The SDS faithfully followed the instructions of the 19th of December Variant A/B. They established an Assembly. And in February 1992 decided to join the ARK, although they'd already been attending meetings of the precursor. And you'll see on the screens before you the decision, 7th of February: "It is hereby proclaimed that the Serbian municipality of Kotor Varos shall be part of the Autonomous District of Krajina ..." Well, of course there wasn't in February a Serbian municipality of Kotor Varos. There was simply Kotor Varos as part of the Bosnian state. In March of 1992, incidents of violence began. The most notorious one was that a JNA reservist shot a Muslim, and as a result, roadblocks were established by the inhabitants of Vrbanjci which was one of the most predominantly Muslim villages. And matters deteriorated so that on the 18th of March, the 122nd Brigade, and indeed other units, were deployed to the wider area of Skender Vakuf and Maslovare. In April of 1992, the weapons were removed from the Kotor Varos TO warehouse and taken to Banja Luka. There was -- there were protests about this, but to no avail. And during May, the 5th Krajina Corps, later to become the 1st Krajina Corps - and as I said, commanded by General Talic - began to deploy forces more heavily in the area. And in March and April a group of Serb police from Kotor Varos went to Banja Luka for what was described as special training. On the 9th of June of 1992, Milos sent a report. And you will see there that: "Following our proposals ..." And let us remind ourselves that Milos was a group working for the SNB in Banja Luka. "... and the proposals of others, the SDS party is due to start an operation soon with the aim of taking over power in the Kotor Varos area and settling ethnic tensions in the Kotor Varos Public Security Station and other organs. Whilst this operation is going on, individuals in possession of unlicensed arms or those they have obtained from the HDZ or the SDA should be handing these arms in. This operation should be carried out in a synchronised manner with the help of the Banja Luka CSB. We shall keep abreast of things and keep you informed about everything in good time." And you will recall that when we looked at the order yesterday about uniforms in the police station, they said with the exception of Kotor Varos and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, to whom was this report sent?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was sent to the head of the SNB who by then was already, I believe, Kesic in the Banja Luka CSB. There was also -- and of course he, then, would report to Stojan Zupljanin. On the 11th of June, which by no accident was the first day of Bajram, which is the big Muslim festival, the 122nd Brigade and members of the Special Police Unit from Banja Luka CSB took part in the take-over of the town of Kotor Varos, Vrbanjci and Dabovci. The Muslims there were told to surrender their arms. This included in the take-over, take-over of the SJB which was headed by Savo Tepic who was a Serb who had been appointed in April of 1992. According to a witness, Tepic was receiving daily instructions during this period from Stojan Zupljanin. The same day the SDS actually formally and openly proclaimed the existence of its Crisis Staff headed by Djukanovic. Some Muslims managed to leave the town and to warn other villages of what had happened. The deputy commander of the SJB, Mr. Sadikovic, who was a Muslim, in fact got away and organised a small band of resistance fighters in the woods, to no avail. On the 12th of June, the village of Hrvacani was attacked with anti-aircraft weapons, mortars, howitzers, and other weapons, and that was followed by other attacks on other villages throughout June. Only two, really, of the villages, namely Vecici and Sokoline, managed to hold out, amazingly enough, until October. Towards the end of June Krajina Television news filmed some of the action that was taking place in Kotor Varos, and we're now going to see that news. You'll need for this, yes, the earphones. And I need some headphones too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's no translation. Okay. I believe the interpreters should be able to interpret this because they've got an English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Are under the control of the Croatian and Muslim extremists. The main organisers of resistance in these areas are well-known criminals Muhamed Berbic and Mehmed Sadikovic. They have a large number of wounded in their ranks and their food reserves are dwindling. The former Ustasha stronghold of Vrbanjci is firmly in the hands of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to take this opportunity to stress that we have encountered exceptional cooperation among these people, but unfortunately, there were two villages where, although we had managed to reach an agreement, units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and members of my unit were fired at and we had to respond accordingly. "Mr. Brdjanin, what are the reasons for your arrival and how would you comment on the recent events in the area of the Kotor Varos municipality? "One of the tasks of the president of an autonomous region Crisis Staff is to visit all the front lines. I must admit that most often I went to the corridor on the way to Serbia. The reason for my arrival is simply the fact that every Monday I have to brief all of the Crisis Staff presidents on the political situation in this area. We must cleanse our area which of course includes Kotor Varos and Jajce. The most important battle being fought at the moment, and I was there yesterday, is the advance towards Serbia. To put it simply, we're now convinced, and we see that ourselves, that there can be no negotiations with those who are waging war against us. Those who have taken up arms must be defeated and return the weapons. Total Serbian rule must be established here. "We have asked the political structures also to take all possible measures to avoid any conflict situations which could lead to the destruction of buildings, loss of life, and so on. However, I must tell you that while the other side has accepted at least partially our activities, a number of extremists have rebelled and refused to place themselves under control or to return their weapons. This surprise visit to the Serbian fighters by the Krajina leaders is a sign of a synchronised operation. Apart from their activities regarding the liberation of Serbian territory, the officers and soldiers of the Serbian armed formations are directly involved in the establishment of the corridor to Serbia as one of the greatest operations in the history of the Serbian people. "... of the police special detachment and three from the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while seven members of the police were slightly wounded. As soon as their wounds were treated they returned to the front lines of their own accord in order to help their comrades crush the last remaining enemy stronghold in Kotor Varos. In today's fighting in Vecici, Muslim and Croat extremists were left with 30 dead and dozens of wounded. Vecici is surrounded by Serbian forces but in the caves and caverns are hardened extremists from the area of the municipality who do not wish to surrender, though they fully understand that none of them can get out. "The mop-up operation continued today in the area of Kotor Varos. In a lightning operation, the members of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre special detachment of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina captured Bilice, one of the most fortified strongholds of the Croatian extremists. Only one member of the special units and army was wounded in this operation, while the enemy had around 50 dead and a large number of wounded. The mop-up is still underway and there are only three more strongholds of Croat Muslims rebels left. The situation in the town itself is gradually returning to normal. Although movement is still allowed only from 9 to 11 hours, life is slowly returning to the streets of Kotor Varos."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honours, we had this checked because there is a break, but it is in fact all Kotor Varos. If there's a dispute, we can deal with the evidence. And there are, as I say, other parts on the take, which we haven't got time to play this afternoon, which show Slobodan, Captain Slobodan Zupljanin, wounded. But I say, we can sort out and we'll double-check that. In fact, we simply wanted to show and there is witness testimony to that effect that particularly in Vecici planes were used and there was bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution's opening statement doesn't form part of the evidence anyway, so let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The attacks, as I say, followed the same pattern. After shelling the Bosnian Serb forces entered the villages, then looted and set fire to houses. And those who survived were captured and taken to the detention facilities. Killings took place during this period. The most notorious was that which took place at the end of June outside the medical centre in Kotor Varos. A number of Muslim men had been brought there and were beaten by members of Kotor Varos MUP, also by the Special Police from Banja Luka, and by soldiers. Following those beatings, 12 to 15 men were executed and one of the witnesses to this event was able to identify one of the killers as a member of the MUP who he knew. The detention facilities in Kotor Varos included a primary school in Maslovare, the SJB, Kotor Varos prison, Kotor Varos school, and most notoriously the sawmill, and you saw those photographs. More important members of the community were actually taken to the CSB Banja Luka. In all these facilities, the prisoners were subjected to different kinds of ill-treatment, ranging from humiliation, beatings, torture, and in the sawmill where women were detained, many of them were raped. The guards for these facilities were largely members of the MUP. The Banja Luka Special Police, in particular three of its members, Ljuban Ecim, Slobodan Dubocanin, whose name you saw on one of those Crisis Staff things, and a man called Zdravko Samardzija, were prominent in the crimes that were committed in Kotor Varos. The Crisis Staff was fully aware of what was happening, as indeed was Stojan Zupljanin. And General Talic also knew because he was receiving daily combat reports. The Crisis Staff held virtually daily, if not sometimes twice-daily, meetings in a building which was a matter of yards from the SJB and they could hear the screams of some of the detainees. The minutes of those meetings record their knowledge, again in a somewhat anodyne fashion. If we look at just a few examples, they kept very -- or we managed to recover a large number of minutes from Kotor Varos. On the 21st of June you will see that they had a meeting. And Savo, who is Savo Tepic: "Highlighted the problem of a lack of personnel for special training of the police." It was concluded that he should invite Ljuban, that's Ljuban Ecim, or Zdravko, that's Samardzija, to the next Crisis Staff meeting and he was then given the task of briefing Stojan Z, we say Stojan Zupljanin, "on problems we are experiencing and scheduling a meeting, attendance at which should be ensured by the following persons Brdjanin, Peulic, and other competent people." Two days later -- three days later, the 24th of June, Inspector Pejic informed the Crisis Staff about the work of the security service and the results of the questioning of the persons who had been brought in. He suggested that a session of the Crisis Staff be devoted to the problem of detained persons. After a discussion of the work of the security station, it was concluded that the Crisis Staff has no right to interfere in the professional work of the police and army, and that no one wishes or requires it to take upon itself security and the creation of conditions for full security on the territory of Kotor Varos municipality ..." And again, it goes back to what I was saying yesterday, that they accepted that there were the lines of -- the chains of authority within the police and army with which they couldn't interfere, although obviously they were going to make suggestions. Next 26th of June, two days later. There you will see that Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic, the VRS commander, was presenting his report. "Savo Tepic informed the Crisis Staff of recent developments in the public security station, and said it was his impression that many members of the special unit were acting without authorisation ..." That's to put it mildly. "... but no one dared criticise them because of the threats that they make ..." And then: "Dr. Gajanin informed the Crisis Staff of the situation as regards casualties and reported on what had been done on the premises of the health centre by members of the special unit, which he had tried to prevent, but was driven away at gunpoint. Nedjo Djekanovic," that's Andjelko Djekanovic, the Crisis Staff president, "said that last night he had told Dubocanin about everything going on at the health centre and in the town and had been assured by him that it would be prevented." In other words, there was clear knowledge, reporting of the crimes that were taking place. "He also said that all these questions had to be cleared up and information provided on the behaviour of the members of the special unit at the meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the CSB, scheduled for tomorrow. Zarko Mikic said that the Crisis Staff had discussed the behaviour of the members of the special unit on several occasions and shown itself unable to influence them and he asked Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic to help solve this problem ..." "At the end of this item, the President said that what had been done yesterday must not happen again and that this kind of behaviour by members of the special unit and individuals on our side must be dealt with and they must be put under control." And I don't actually think we need to -- this was simply an example of the use of language, but I don't think we need to -- given the time. If we move to the next Crisis Staff meeting, 29th of June, item 2: "In the health centre, six people have been recorded as killed and 19 wounded." That was very short of the true figure. "With regard to the activities of the Crisis Staff members, the following conclusions: "All those willing to move out of Kotor Varos are to make a statement at the lower court leaving their immovable property to the social and political community ..." And then going down further: "Detainees are to be held at the warehouse Pilana," which is sawmill. "And Mr. Gavric is to take part in the Crisis Staff and take responsibility for organising population resettlement." So we've got everything in this one, we've got the killings, moving out, and the detention facilities. Has the next one got up? Yeah. And then on Friday, the 28th of August, and we'll be looking at some slightly different ones later, there is a report from Captain Zupljanin and then in the middle of that paragraph Chief Sepic [sic], it's one line further up. That's it. Chief Tepic reported about visiting the branch and whatever, and insisted that the names of police officers who had been engaged in unauthorised dealings and then: "He informed the War Presidency that on the basis of the instructions of the CSB a proposal has been prepared that people should be released from prison ..." That relates to two matters. First, throughout August, as you will hear during the evidence, the republican-level government was making -- producing reports designed to look at the detention centres in order to deal with the international outcry over these detention centres. And all police authorities were ordered to report on numbers of the prisoners and the like. But the second thing is this, it shows that Stojan Zupljanin, at the CSB, had the authority to order the release of prisoners, even in Kotor Varos. Yeah. And then I think finally on this little group, this is a 1st Krajina Corps document. They also engaged in regular reporting, and under item 4, "Situation on the ground," it talks about the 20th Light Infantry Brigade, which is the one that covered Kotor Varos, is stressing that there is resentment among the population because of the attack on the Muslim village of Koricani. "The same command has detected an Ustasha group consisting of about 30 Ustashas in the Bilice village near Kotor Varos and is undertaking measures to destroy them. The Banja Luka CSB Security Services Centre special detachment located in the Kotor Varos area has still not joined the 22nd Light Brigade and is causing serious problems on the ground." Everybody -- it was a public scandal the behaviour of the special police from Banja Luka. In fact, so notorious had the special police become that Stojan Zupljanin had been requested that they be withdrawn, but in fact, as will be seen, they were still operating at the end of August. It may be that we can skip some of these because it should move backwards. Yes, I think we -- can we put that one, 14th of July? It's going slightly backwards again, but 14th of July, Kotor Varos again, and in item 1, the War Presidency concluded it was not satisfied with the results achieved so far and the current military and security situation. It was further concluded that General Talic and Stojan Zupljanin have to be contacted urgently in order to inform them of our dissatisfaction. Item 2: "Activities relating to moving out the population failed to meet expectations. This task must be dealt with in a much more organised fashion; an agency has to be established to handle these matters." 24th of July, still on the subject of what is called re-settlement of population and what we say was in fact the forced expulsion of non-Serbs. Remember we heard Mr. Gavric in one of the other meetings. He was to compile and forward to the Presidency a detailed report on the re-settlement of the population, number of convoys, number of persons, profile of those who moved out, who did the transporting, and so on and so forth. On the 28th of July, again the Crisis Staff was aware that through the report from the chief of the SJB, who was also aware, that: "... confiscating the money of individuals who are moving out, it was established that this was being done without anyone's order, i.e., in an unauthorised manner and this can have a negative effect on the operation and reputation of all of us. It was decided that the money confiscated in this manner will be used to help the families of soldiers killed and other essential costs of the municipality." Some people might have thought that perhaps the money should be returned to those from whom it had been stolen. And then the 28th of July, this is a Krajina report, and it shows the, as it were, the -- the authorities working as of one mind. "In the city of Banja Luka and other large towns there is an increased demand for, and organisation of, the departure of Croatian and Muslim population. We consider that the municipal and regional authorities should work much harder at this." And then on the 21st of August the War Presidency: " ... President Djekanovic pointed out matters and problems to be solved, to the effect that pressure and provocation by certain members of the special forces unit directed against the Muslim and Croat families in order to compel them to leave should be stopped; that the question of what to do with several families from Gornji Cepak who cannot stay here but are still in Cepak should be dealt with and that the killing of the Orsulic couple should be investigated." Now, the special police was supposed to have been withdrawn back in July. They were still operating in August, and then I think that will -- perhaps we can just look at the 19th of August which is attached to the back of 745. And item 2: "Slobodan Zupljanin and Mane Tepic briefed the War Presidency, the situation of the ground military ..." "Zupljanin also informed the Presidency about the results of the meeting with General Talic ... corps commander and what had been agreed with him." So they were getting full reports all the way through. The forced transfer or deportation of the non-Serb population was overseen by the municipal authorities, but they recorded all their actions as being carried out on orders. First of all, can we look at an example of the doc -- sort of document that somebody leaving was supposed to sign. All of that information. And going down to the next two -- yes -- no, above that. Yeah. "I hereby declare ... I'm voluntarily leaving Kotor Varos" -- "I wish to move away ..." et cetera, et cetera. " ... And I leave behind my land in Kotor and my destroyed house ..." And then he says he will not fight against the ensuance of the Serbian republic. And then can we look at the last paragraph. "This statement is done in three identical copies, one of which will be sent to the Crisis Staff, one to the population re-settlement agency ..." And you will recall that they were saying agency should be set up. One indeed was set up. " ... and one to the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And then finally in October 1992 the War Presidency in Kotor Varos lasted longer than almost anywhere else because the residents of Vecici held out so long. And you will see that he, Nedjeljko Djekanovic, talked about the weapons surrender. This was all to do with Vecici. And then he said: "As for the action of surrendering weapons and movings of people from the territory of Kotor Varos, he pointed out that the drive and all activities had been conducted on the orders of the Government and the Presidency of the Republika Srpska ..." By 1994 when the Banja Luka conducted a survey of the populations, they showed the -- what it was in 1991, the figures which I gave you earlier, and you will see that there'd been an increase in Serbs. Now, these are approximate figures, admittedly, and Muslims had gone from 11.000, just over 11.000, to just under 2. And Croats from 10.000 to under a thousand. And as far as the cultural property is concerned, the evidence will show that most, if not all, Roman Catholic churches and mosques in the Kotor Varos municipality were destroyed in 1992. The film that you saw and, as I said, it was the village of Vecici that held out until the end of October. On the 2nd of November, and you heard the commentator talking about the fact they knew that they were surrounded and couldn't escape. On the 2nd of November a group of about 200 men tried to escape while the women and children surrendered. They were ambushed and about 150 were captured. Others were killed there and then, and they were taken to a school in Grabovica together with the women and children who'd surrendered. And the latter, the women and children, were taken away on buses provided by the Crisis Staff. The men were then executed by members of the military. No members of the police, I hasten to add, were involved in that killing. And accordingly, that's why it's not charged in this indictment, but nonetheless, it's part of the general picture of what happened in this municipality. The killings were recorded by the VRS in the -- their daily combat report of the 4th of November, and the Crisis Staff minutes record that Mr. Djekanovic, the president, went to the school on the 5th of November to assist in, as described, cleansing. Can I -- having looked in a little detail now at Kotor Varos, can I then turn to other examples that you're going to hear about in this case of the major killings. In Prijedor the take-over and the subsequent attacks followed much the same pattern as Kotor Varos, they actually happened earlier. The names of the villages have become infamous, Kozarac in particular. Large numbers of civilians were killed during and after the attacks. In 1996 -- thank you -- in 1996 members of the Office of the Prosecutor -- I think it's 1996, is it -- yes -- were allowed in for the first time with cameras. And I'm just going to show you a very brief shot of what Kozarac looked like in 1996. And there's no sound -- I'm so sorry. There's no sound to this. It's just some ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who took the footage?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor. Slow down. Yeah. Any houses remaining standing, we heard from the evidence, were nearly all owned by Serbs. Okay. Speed that up. Kozarac was shelled before the troops went in. Okay. Let's fast-forward to the remains of the mosque. And what you see there is the minaret, I believe. The cultural expert will be better -- and of one of the mosques in Kozarac. There are -- there is film taken by news reporters at the time, but this is perhaps the clearest. The two major killings associated with the municipality was the massacre -- and it was room 3, and I ought to have known that, of Keraterm camp which was a disused ceramics factory on the outskirts of Prijedor. The guards were members of Prijedor SJB. They assisted in or they allowed men who were armed with automatic weapons into the building and, as I said, opened fire on the detainees who came from the Brdo area of Prijedor municipality which had been recently, as it were, cleansed, and more than a hundred people were killed. The bodies have never been recovered. And in August of 1992, trucks and buses which were taking Muslim men, women, and children from the Prijedor area were being escorted by members of the Prijedor police so-called intervention platoon, which was another form of special police. The convoy was stopped. The men were separated by the police. They were driven to a mountainous area in Skender Vakuf called Mount Vlasic, Koricanske Stijene. The other men were taken out to the edge of a cliff and shot. Only 200 -- out of 200 men only a handful survived. It was one of the most notorious events of the whole war and in the end of what I have to say we will look at something that happened. We just thought you might like to have a look at some photographs of what this place looks like, taken very recently, in fact, in June -- taken earlier. All right. Taken at some stage. It's just to show you what it looks like. There's the road and it is, you may think, amazing that anybody was able to survive. That's Prijedor. In Kljuc, the attacks on the Muslim villages also resulted in two major killings. On June the 1st Muslim men had been detained in a school in Velagici. It was guarded by Bosnian Serb police and the army. Shortly before midnight the detainees were ordered to line up in front of the school, and two Serb soldiers opened fire killing at least 77. On the 10th of July special police and soldiers rounded up the inhabitants of the Biljani area, and again confined them in a school. The men, between 150 and 200 were killed, some at the school, some in a nearby house, and some -- and others elsewhere. In Bosanski Samac, on the 17th of May, 18 detainees in a warehouse which were guarded by police were killed by members of a paramilitary group. The police ordered the other detainees to load the bodies on to a truck, then took them to an area where the survivors were forced by the police to bury the bodies. In Gacko in August, Bosnian Serb police and soldiers took detainees from the SJB building to a bridge at Kotlina and nine were shot and killed. In Zvornik on about the 30th of May, Muslim detainees from the village of Kostijerevo were being detained in a school building. The men were beaten, tortured, and then executed in groups of ten. 88 men were killed. On the 1st of June, 750 Muslim men were taken to a technical school which was guarded by the police. Men suffocated in a hangar. 160 of those who survived were taken out and killed. The remainder were transferred on the 5th of June to a cinema hall, and groups were taken from there to a slaughter-house on three different occasions and killed. In Visegrad, the Lukics, Milan and Sredoje, the trial of who has just finished, were the most active proponents of the cleansing operation. Their group was originally part of the reserve police force. In June Milan Lukic executed five non-Serb men on the banks of the river Drina, and a week later, having confined more than 60 civilians, including women, in a house they doused it with inflammable liquid and setting it on fire, causing the death of most. In Brcko although the killings were not on the sort of massive scale that I've just been describing, they were widespread and extremely scandalous. One of the most notorious killers was a member of the MUP. In fact, he was put in charge of a detention camp there called Goran Jelisic, and the photographs of what he did have become almost as infamous as those way back in the Vietnam war when we show the police captain shooting somebody. What we see here is Jelisic is the man in short sleeves holding the gun, and we see there is another armed man behind him. He fires the gun at the Muslim, and again. And we see the death of the men. Your Honours, it's probably time, I think, for a break. I've -- I'm coming on to detention facilities, and I will complete certainly my opening before 6.00.
