utterances.text: My both accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was about to say during the course of the break, I've been inviting the Defence to obviously correct me if I'm saying anything that's to their certain knowledge not agreed or incorrect. But Mr. Zecevic approached me about the question of Goran Jelisic and his membership of the police. I understand that will be a matter of dispute. I was referred to the Jelisic judgement which we pulled up very quickly and it says he was given police duties. But in any event I wouldn't like Your Honours -- as Judge Harhoff just pointed out, what I say is not evidence, and Your Honours will undoubtedly listen to the evidence, but Mr. Zecevic drew that to my attention. Can I turn, then, to the broad outline of the detention facilities that you will hear about in this case. Again, this is just examples. All of the detention facilities which are charged in this indictment had some kind of police presence there. Some were entirely police detention centres; others, such as Manjaca, was largely the province of the army, the VRS, but contained an element of guards from the MUP. And we have a diagram which we'll quickly show you where the names and where these -- of the detention camps in the municipalities which are going to be dealt with in this indictment. As with the killings, the most notorious detention facilities were those in the Prijedor region, namely Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Omarska was established on the 31st of May by the direct order of Simo Drljaca. The commander of Omarska was a man named Zeljko Mejakic, who came from the Omarska sub-police station. If one looks quickly at the documents setting up the camp, dated the 31st of May of 1992: "The industrial compound of the 'Omarska' mine-strip shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the Security Services' operational information." That of course gave it a semblance of legitimacy. Could we go over to paragraph 6 on the next page. Okay. Don't worry. We -- through my mistake, we haven't got that in, but I'll just say that the security was to be provided by the Omarska police station. They had to report, as you will hear, every 24 hours or immediately when circumstances allow no delay. The author, Simo Drljaca, prohibited the giving of any information whatsoever concerning the function of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor Public Security Station. And then the last page -- don't worry, that's my fault. Last page. All right. Rather than -- don't worry. It's signed by Simo Drljaca and copies went to the -- among other people the security services centre in Banja Luka. Ah, there we are. Simo Drljaca, a man of considerable notoriety, in particular because when an attempt was made to arrest him by SFOR way, way back, in 1996, he was shot. The camp Omarska held thousands of Muslim and Croat civilians, including women. The prisoners were regularly beaten and tortured, some during interrogations which were carried out by members of the MUP. People died from the beatings carried out not only by guards but by people they allowed to enter the camp. Women were raped. As I've said earlier, the conditions were atrocious, overcrowding, lack of food and water and sanitary facilities, with very limited medical care. The camp was actually visited in July by the Banja Luka authorities which included both Stojan Zupljanin and Radoslav Brdjanin. Radoslav Brdjanin described to a reporter what he found in his visit as an example of a job well done. That was his overall visit to Prijedor. Keraterm, which was actually established a few days earlier, reflected the same types of crimes. Trnopolje was in a slightly different category, in that it contained, apart from people who'd been detained, dispossessed families who'd been sent there or taken there. Eventually when Omarska and Keraterm were closed at the beginning of August, the inmates were transferred to Trnopolje, which remained open until November and the detainees who'd not been killed or transported out of the country were then transported to Batkovic camp in Bijeljina, and that in itself, because they were also transported to that same camp from other camps in other areas of Bosnia, is a demonstration that this was a carefully conceived and worked-out enterprise. However, also in Trnopolje there were beatings which led to death and women were raped. It was these camps, in particular Omarska and Trnopolje, that were visited at the beginning of August by international reporters. And the film that they produced not only led to the closure of these camps, but as I mentioned earlier, provided the outside world with the first real evidence of what was happening in that part of Bosnia. And I think it's worth just playing, although it's been seen over and over again, the particular film. It was filmed by ITN and the reporter was a woman named Penny Marshall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] These are the Muslim prisoners of Omarska. In small groups, under heavy Serbian guard, they are ushered into the canteen for their single meal of the day. Most have been here for two months. They say they don't know why but they were rounded up from their homes. They were too frightened to talk about the way they have been treated and the conditions in which they have been kept. Conditions which have been hidden from the world, as the Serbs have denied access here to the United Nations and to the International Red Cross. Their prison is an old mining complex outside Banja Luka in northern Bosnia. In an office above the canteen, the camp commandant and a spokeswoman for the local" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to point out that the person you're seeing in the uniform is, in fact, Simo Drljaca

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Serbian authorities said they had two and a half thousand of what they called internees who were being interrogated as possible Muslim fighters. "No, this is not a camp. This is a centre, a target centre, Omarska and Trnopolje, both [indiscernible] centres not camps. "The prisoners were being brought to the canteen from a large industrial building in the centre of the mining complex. It too was under heavy guard and we asked to be allowed to look inside. But in spite of promises of openness from the Serb Bosnian leader Dr. Karadzic, we were told we could see no more. "Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "He -- he promised us something else and said, You can do this and this and that, and not that. "Our armed escort made it clear. Our visit was over. "We're now being asked to leave this camp having seen nothing more than the canteen. We have been told that Dr. Karadzic's promise, while good to us, does not carry any weight here. "As we were moved on, soldiers told us the army did not control the camp, which they said was run by the local authorities and militia. "We had asked to be taken to a second camp at Trnopolje, in the same area, to which several hundred prisoners from Omarska had that day been transferred and which has also been at the centre of allegations of atrocities. Conditions at this camp were appalling. In 100-degree heat, hundreds of men were forced to eat and sleep outside in the field, behind barbed wire. Their meager rations consist of a small hunk of bread and a bowl of soup every day. Here too they said they had been rounded, whole villages emptied of their men, and they were afraid. "Can you tell me anything about the conditions in which you are being kept here or is it difficult? "I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that. You know, I'm -- can you understand me? "Have people here been beaten? "Here? No. Here, no. Not here. "[Indiscernible] "I rather wouldn't talk about that. I'm sure ... "Can you tell us anything about the conditions that you are being kept in and the treatment of the people you were with? "Well, that was hard time, how can I say but ... "We heard stories of people being beaten and people disappearing. Was that -- did that happen? "Well, I can't say much about that. "We just came here. "From another camp? "From another camp and we didn't know what the condition here. We accept a little bit more -- better. "What were you -- "Like a prison. "What was it like before? "It was terrible. "One of the prisoners asked us to check on him in several days' time to see that he hadn't been punished for speaking to us, and away from the camera there were allegations of routine beatings and executions. Several prisoners told us of retaliatory killings. One instance in which they claimed 150 of their fellow prisoners had been killed following the death of ten Serbian soldiers in a Muslim village. We were told people had been beaten to death, and we were asked to smuggle a film out of the camp. The pictures show severe injuries, apparently as a result of beatings. "In the makeshift medical centre there were cases of scabies, malnutrition and diarrhea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicine and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings. "[Indiscernible] "On one side of the camp were refugees who were here simply because they have nowhere else to go, their homes having been destroyed. They have been told they can go as soon as they have a guarantee of a home outside Serb-controlled Bosnia. In Banja Luka prisoners' wives have been queuing for days for news of their men and to register as refugees, because they too have nowhere to go. On the roads to Banja Luka, Muslim villages lie empty and deserted. Homes destroyed. "If there is eventually freedom for the men in the detention centres, it's unlikely to be in Serb-controlled Bosnia. "Ian Williams, ITN, northern Bosnia. "And Ian Williams joins us now live. "Ian, you were clearly supervised as you went" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There is other video evidence as part of the exhibits in this case which shows more pictures of the camps. The evidence shows also that the doctor who you saw there was the person who asked the reporters to smuggle the film out of the beaten boy that you saw. Manjaca camp was just outside Banja Luka. It was, in fact, originally a military training-ground and it operated from May until December. As I said, it was operated largely by the VRS military police under the command of a retired then brought back colonel called Popovic. But members of the MUP secured the camp's perimeter and indeed conducted the interrogations of people who were held there. Again, conditions in that camp were appalling and people died because of the beatings. Most famously a Muslim called Omer Filipovic who came from Kljuc. Many of the people rounded up from Kljuc and Sanski Most in particular ended up in Manjaca, and again, Manjaca camp was actually visited at the time by Lord Ashdown. And indeed, an earlier -- also one of the prisons in Sarajevo Kula. And I'm afraid the quality of the sound in this video is very bad. Again, it's a newsreel. I believe CNN, because I think the reporter is Christiane Amanpour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... has been a prison for the last 20 years and it is not on the list of detention centres that outside observers have requested to see, yet this is where the first international observer has been brought. He is Paddy Ashdown, leader of Britain's Liberal Democrat party. He was invited by the president of Bosnian Serbs, Radovan Karadzic, under great pressure since reports of Serbian concentration camps made world headlines. Karadzic made a great show of standing aside while Ashdown interviewed these prisoners. "There's never been any concern about the way this particular camp is run, but I do want to suspend my judgement until I see some of the other camps. "And Karadzic chose this moment to make his first so-called unilateral gesture of goodwill releasing just ten prisoners, those who are over 60 or in poor health. Smiling he handed out release papers as though he were handing out awards and he brought tears of joy to those who were being freed. "The Serbs say they hold a maximum of 8.250 prisoners, not the 58.000 that the opposition claims. They say they would like to get rid of all of them, but, say the Serbs, they have had no reciprocal gestures from the Muslims or the Croats. "We release people who are not likely to be mobilised again. If we release all of those people without exchange they will be mobilised immediately and they will fight against us. It would be unreasonable. "The Serbs say all the people here are fighters. The prisoners say they are not. "I have no weapons. I didn't shoot. "This man is blind in one eye. He says he couldn't fight even if he wanted to. They all say they've been taken as bargain [indiscernible] for prisoners from the other side, and they don't expect to be released any time soon. "Christiane Amanpour at Kula prison, outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The conditions in which --" "[Voiceover]... Paddy Ashdown had broken his holiday and travelled for three days over a thousand miles to get to Manjaca camp. What he saw was a shed which in better days might have housed animals now home to more than 600 men. Here the prisoners live, eat and sleep 24 hours a day. Most of these men just arrived three days ago from the camp at Omarska. Their faces still haunted by memories they did not dare relate in the presence of their guard. For five minutes, Paddy Ashdown was allowed to speak privately to the men. However grim their conditions here, they told him, things were much better than the place they'd just come from. The camp commandant had promised Mr. Ashdown total freedom to see anything he wanted. In the event he was told that wasn't possible. "Even during Mr. Ashdown's visit time was limited to a mere half-hour and access was limited to only a few prisoners. "As he left he said however bleak things seem to be, this camp did appear to be properly run. "Clearly I have had access to those prisoners without the guards present. I [indiscernible] them, and I find them deeply moving. They have had an appalling time in Omarska where they've come from. I think it's a tremendous improvement on the part of the press that have exposed that, and they've probably just saved very many prisoners' lives. But every prisoner I've spoke to here without the guards present have told me conditions are not what you'd want them to be but they're a hell of a lot better than they had been before. "With the visiting politician gone, what these men have suffered in the past remains largely unspoken. "Caroline [indiscernible], Manjaca prison camp in Bosnia. "[Indiscernible] -- camp in Serbian-held northern Bosnia. Authorities say they hold 3500 prisoners here, including about a thousand from the --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thanks. I think we're just repeating the same clip, Your Honours. Your Honours will hear from people in one form or another, whether in writing or whatever, from those incarcerated in Manjaca and contrary to what Lord Ashdown, as he later became, thought conditions were considerably worse than it would appear. Some of the prisoners who were transported to Manjaca from the other detention facilities, including Betonirka in Sanski Most and Omarska, died during the transport through the conditions of that transport. In fact, that prompted a remarkably honest report from one of the VR officers -- VRS officers who were stationed in Manjaca. And if you look now at that report dated the 7th of August. Prisoners of war, military secret, strictly classified, and it's addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps command, the security and intelligence department. If you go to the second paragraph: "We received the prisoners of war from 'Omarska' camp. The reception has been organised but not followed since no paperwork. A total of eight prisoners died during the transport from Omarska to Manjaca, three of which have most probably been killed because they had visible traces of violence. We did not receive prisoners and we insisted that they are driven back to Omarska for proper burial there. However, it is very probable that the dead have been loaded off and thrown somewhere in the forest on the Manjaca-Banja Luka strip. "The behaviour of people who participated in securing the transportation of the prisoners is very incorrect, inhuman, and bullying. So when the security organ warned them not to kill a half-dead prisoner they told him, 'Should you act like that, you'll get what he got.' "Indeed it is obvious that the world public is not complaining without arguments, because it is us who provide those arguments. I am requesting the organs of the 1st Krajina Corps command to take care on their own level and in their sphere of competence for similar scenes never to happen again. "Manjaca camp is now full and has no room for a single prisoner. We are reminding that the investigating inspector's explanation was that all prisoners who have been brought from 'Omarska' are 'serious extremists,' and that he didn't provide a single fact in explanation of that fact. During the reception, we have found people who weren't even fit to hold a rifle in their hands, nonetheless to run or to shoot. We also found minors, born in 1977, who didn't even have a weapon or participated in the combat, not even being water carriers to the enemy. All of this is indicative of thoughtless conduct of the organ in Prijedor and the superficial work of the organs of the police and the SUP. This is the reason why we are requesting you urgently give us the official records of the interviews with the prisoners." And last paragraph: "Considering that there are minors, individuals older than 60, and sick individuals among the newly arrived prisoners (from Omarska), there is a need to make lists and ... after we process them to suggest they're released with the mediation of the Red Cross." We suggest that that corroborates what the evidence shows that there was just whole-scale round-up of people who were not Serb going on and had nothing whatsoever to do with combat activities. As a result of the international furore which attended the revelation of these detention facilities, Karadzic issued an order about the treatment of prisoners and this prompted Stojan Zupljanin to send an order to SJB chiefs. And you see that on the -- well, first of all, it's Karadzic's order, first of all, that's coming up on the screen. We'll just go to the next page. Signed Karadzic. And then same -- same day, Stojan Zupljanin to the chiefs. Necessary for all public security stations transporting prisoners of war to Manjaca to start assembling personal files for each prisoner of war individually. Again, in parenthesis, one might have thought that someone might have done that before. "To ensure expeditious execution of this task, on the 20th of August, operatives should be sent to Manjaca with the documents collected so far ... number -- in consideration of the numbers of prisoners, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc ... should each send a team of operatives ..." and they must report. In Vlasenica, turning to a different area, the most notorious camp was Susica under the command of Dragan Nikolic, a member of the special police. Detainees were beaten, robbed, tortured, and killed. Female detainees were raped. Again, some prisoners were transferred to Batkovic. On the 30th of September, Karadzic made a speech at a funeral of some VRS people being killed, and it seems to be particularly inflammatory, and that night members of the MUP at the Susica camp executed the detainees that remained. Again, that is not part of the indictment, but it is part of the general picture of what happened in Susica. Every single municipality had its share of detention facilities, and in each the pattern of beatings, killings, and inhuman conditions were repeated. In Pale where the Bosnian Serbs had an overwhelming majority and was indeed the seat of the Republika Srpska government and for a period the MUP was based there, indeed so Mico Stanisic was there, detained -- the MUP detained and beat non-Serbs from the SJB -- in the SJB building and a gym in the old cultural centre. So that's a brief survey of the detention facilities that figure in this case. A word about paramilitaries and the RS MUP. The relationship between the RS MUP and the paramilitary formations which operated during this period could really be described as love/hate, the same between the VRS and the paramilitary formations. There was cooperation between these paramilitaries and the authorities when it was useful to them. But once they wanted to establish law and order in the territories that they were -- had brought under Bosnian Serb control, then these paramilitaries became a nuisance or a lot worse, and particularly when they started to attack property and persons of Bosnian Serbs. In the original seizures of power, paramilitary formations worked side by side with the RS MUP and the VRS. And this was particularly marked in Sanski Most, in Bosanski Samac, in Visegrad, Donji Vakuf, and in Zvornik. Arkan's men figured particularly in Zvornik. However, quite often thereafter the paramilitaries remained in the area even after they'd -- the areas had come under Serb -- Bosnian and Serb control, and they committed crimes and therefore became an embarrassment to the authorities. In Zvornik, a group calling themselves the Yellow Wasps were heavily engaged in the torture and death of inmates in detention facilities. They were allowed in by members of the MUP who'd been guarding those facilities. No action, however, was taken against them until they started to cause problems to the SJB in Zvornik. And in -- there is a report, a very, very lengthy report put in by the chief on the activities of the Zvornik public security station over the three months July to September 1992. Paragraph 2: " ... the station opposite -- until July 30th this year," that's when action was taken against the Yellow Wasps, "this station operated in very difficult circumstances and was unable to operate ... because of large and small paramilitary groups which operated on the territory of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik, rendering the activities of the station, as well as other state organs impossible ... "They created a psychosis of fear," et cetera, "and uncertainty among the citizens in the city, which made it possible for goods of various quantities and value to be taken out of the municipality," and there's a list of those goods. "Because of all this, in order to improve the overall security situation and find a role and a place for the station in accordance with the law, a special MUP unit," that was special police "was engaged, which at the end of July dispersed the paramilitary groups and enabled the station to assume its role as defined by the law." And incidentally while we're on that going a bit further down, although it's not on the same topic: "A string of measures and activities were undertaken in order to resolve -- solve the issue of collection centres of which there are two ... about 180 people in them. The municipal organs, military organs, CSB, MUP, and Ministry of Health ... were informed about this problem, but it still remains unresolved ..." And I think that's all we need. As I say, it's a very lengthy report. Once again -- in Teslic, and again, I'm just giving a couple of examples really, a group called the Mice went into the area in June 1992. They actually were carrying identification -- identity cards from both the military and the police. One of the leaders of this group Milan Savic was a high-ranking officer in the CSB Doboj. They appear to have been sent there to encourage the Teslic authorities to speed up the process, and they took it upon themselves to arrest and detain and then beat up and finally kill non-Serbs. This they were allowed to do without any hindrance from the authorities in Teslic or without the Teslic authorities seeking any help until the Serb population began to complain. As a result, the Teslic authorities went to Banja Luka and they applied to Stojan Zupljanin for assistance in getting rid of the group. Stojan Zupljanin sent a member of the SNB in Banja Luka, a man called Predrag Radulovic. He took a force of men with him and arrested members of the group. They were originally detained in Banja Luka prison, but they were then ordered to be transferred to Doboj prison where they were promptly released. And one of the matters I'll deal with in a moment or two is the failure to really deal properly with anybody that was arrested. And the events in Teslic were really rather pithily summed up by the Prosecutor from Teslic in his report to the Municipal Assembly in September of 1992. If we come down to the second section manifest forms of crime the part that begins: "The public Prosecutor's office received crime reports against 112 persons during the report period. All crime reports were dealt with in a timely fashion. Investigations were requested against 81 persons ..." And so on and so forth. Again, this is an issue I'll return to, but there's no doubt at all that the criminal justice system can't have been working perfectly through this period but it was certainly working. If we go over the page, you'll see the numbers at the top and then of the paragraph just below the chart: "Of the persons reported, 85 were Muslims, 27 were Serbs, and no crime reports against Croats. The Muslims were reported for armed rebellion and the illegal possession of weapons or explosives, while the Serbs were reported for all other criminal acts." And we can see what they were, aggravated larceny, five for murder, and then illegal deprivation of freedom. "All the Serbs reported were members of the Serbian army formation or reserve policemen." Actual crime situation. "Recorded crime is a fraction ... most criminal acts remain undiscovered, and many crimes are tolerated by the authorities for various reasons. The Prosecutor's office has knowledge of the day-to-day looting of property, houses, business premises being set on fire and destroyed, armed robbery and murder being committed for base motives, socially owned flats and private houses being occupied unlawfully, stealing of forest timber, and other forms of wilful act. There is no criminal prosecution for most of these acts. In ten days alone there were three murders for base motives and several cases of arson and armed robbery. In only one case were the perpetrators arrested and criminal proceedings initiated against them. The perpetrators of the other two murders have not been arrested to the present day. The public Prosecutor, president of the court personally demanded the command of the Teslic Serbian brigade arrest one accomplice on suspicion of murder. It is inexplicable why these people have not been arrested." Go over the page, top paragraph. "The destruction of religious buildings is a war crime against civilians because of the way and circumstances in which it was perpetrated. The Serbian people will carry a heavy burden of historical responsibility until the perpetrators of these and similar criminal acts are brought to justice." And the job of whom was it to bring these people to justice? The police. Over the course of the last session -- a day and a bit or whatever one calls it, I've dealt with a quite a number of parts of the evidence and documents that we say shows evidence of the participation in the joint criminal enterprise by both accused. Both Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin were men of great authority, not only by virtue of the positions which they held but also through the nature of their personalities. The RS MUP, like the VRS, was a strongly hierarchical organisation. We've already seen that Stojan Zupljanin was writing that his word was law. And Mico Stanisic made his position no less clear in an interview that he gave to Javnost on the 30th of October of 1992. You see the date at the top, and then: "Rule of law established." And then we have the reporter asking him -- pointing -- asking him about the appointment to these -- to the position. And in the answer about halfway down through the answer -- sorry, I should have said the question is: "Bearing in mind specific wartime circumstances to what extent are you satisfied with the activities of the organs of the internal affairs of the Republika Srpska?" And he says: "We are among the first organs which were set up in quite an organised manner as part of the executive power in the territory of our state. Notwithstanding all organisational difficulties, I want to point out that I am really satisfied with the way the interior ministry is functioning and that I am satisfied with the level of our organisation, especially with the dedication and determination of all the members of our service to make their utmost contribution to the cause which the ... Serbian people are fighting for." He was asked about the tactical equipment. And on the next page -- yes. He was asked: "Are there any problems of coordination between the organs of the Ministry of the Interior in different areas ... namely, is the functioning of the service in these war times utterly centralised? "Fortunately," replied Mr. Stanisic, "the Ministry of the Interior indeed functions as a centralised organ and we do not sense any autonomous or secessionist tendencies amongst the members or our service." That must be it. "Every briefing that I hold is attended by my assistants, assistant secretaries, chiefs of security services centres from all the areas. It has not happened yet that we had a briefing which was not attended by all the staff members regardless of the location where the briefing took place. "Also," this is the part that we wish to stress, "it has not happened yet that anyone in the whole territory of Republika Srpska ever refused to carry out any of my orders issued, of course, in accordance with the law." I would like to -- I think the next bit -- if we go down the page a bit. "I think that nowadays we are the only ministry some members of which have been expelled from our ranks - not because they did anything against the Serbian interest but because they committed individual acts succumbing to base instincts which really does not befit a member of our service. "How many such cases are there? "Such cases are rare, but significant /sic/ for us. We want a ministry without a single member who would disregard the legal norms of Republika Srpska." We say that was deliberate disinformation being given to the people. Have you got the next page? We just -- there's one part of the next page perhaps we might look at. Page 3, sorry, that's it. At the bottom the question was: "Some are inclined to accuse the special units of the Ministry of the Interior of abuse of power when performing their duties in Bijeljina." Then there is a bit about: "We are determined to protect our constitutional order ..." et cetera. "Anyone who decides to disturb the above-mentioned has to be aware that we are categorically going to use all available legal measures to prevent and defeat such attempts. It is not true that the special unit abused power in Bijeljina." Again, the evidence will show that that also was not true. Both of the accused were what is generally known as hands-on leaders. We've already seen footage of Stojan Zupljanin in the field at Kotor Varos, footage of Mico Stanisic with his men, Special Police, on their training exercises. There are other film clips of Stanisic, particularly one in October 1992, where he's interviewed clearly, as it were, on the field of battle. Mico Stanisic attended sessions of the government in which policy was discussed and he himself participated in the discussions. And if we just look at one example. These are the minutes of the 41st Session held on the 22nd of July. We see there attending Mico Stanisic. The agenda begins there. We see over the page everything. And then in particular, can I draw Your Honours' attention to 7 and 8: "Proposal for appointing a president to the Central Commission for the Exchange of War Prisoners. "Agreement on the conditions and way of exchanging war prisoners." As you will hear during the evidence that central commission was another device for expelling the non-Serbs. If we go down further on, on the same page, Mico Stanisic is raising a question on why the minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Buha, isn't present. Over the page, Momcilo Mandic was also there and he's proposing that that Mico Stanisic be appointed a member of the commission. And then Mico Stanisic speaks again further down the page, all to do with the -- this commission. And I don't think that -- as I say, the full document, you -- it's matters of policy outside the strict area of the Ministry of the Interior. It also appeared to other members of the government that Mico Stanisic had a particularly close relationship with Radovan Karadzic and also Momcilo Krajisnik, and he therefore bypassed the normal chain of command in the government in that Mico Stanisic should have gone to the prime minister of the government. And there -- that impression may have been gained by people around them. He was also filmed going to places with them. In fact, Branko Djeric, the prime minister, publicly complained about Mico Stanisic's avoidance of the normal chain of command in the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 23rd of November. And if we go to page 17, this is a long speech by Mr. Djeric. It began two pages earlier. And he says -- no, we go to the next -- yeah. "For example, when it comes to the justice system, when it comes to the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Internal Affairs" -- the minister of justice was Mandic, "they are not even in the government. They never come to the government sessions, only to the president of the republic or the president of the Assembly. Neither of them has ever stood up in front of the people or on television and said: 'We are responsible for their work,' which would release the prime minister from the responsibility." I think this was -- taken as a whole it was a complaint that he getting blamed for things that he really ought not to have got blamed for. And Stanisic responded, starting at page 19, long speech again, and then on the last part he said in the paragraph, page 21, yes. I can let you know, that's the one. "I can let you know about our financial affairs," blah, blah, blah, "you know, "he said, "that the police have built this country from the beginning, along with the people, defending them and providing space for the government to make law regulations and to turn this country into a legal state. I am always ready to present to you all that we have done during the period. There were no regulations ..." Well, that certainly wasn't true. We have already seen that there was regulation after regulation and order being issued. "... the intentions were good, but if there were any mistakes we are ready to discuss them and to answer for them. Therefore, I do not agree that anyone can say, call someone to be Radovan's man, and based on that to claim he is no good." And this was a remarkable admission. "We had to also take criminals and crooks, because you know that no intellectual took the rifle in his hand and went to fight for his country. We had good intentions. If I was wrong, I accept this ..." That of course is part of the case for the Prosecution, that knowingly and deliberately that the police used, took into their ranks, people who they knew were criminals and were likely to commit criminal offences and did nothing about it. Mico Stanisic, as we've seen already, issued orders to the CSB chiefs he appointed and to the RS MUP generally. As we've already seen, he required prompt action and reporting thereof. We've looked at some examples, but another example of a major order was the one issued on the 27th of July, which included the disbandment of the CSB Special Units and the creation of one single Special Police unit. This was issued on the 27th of July, and item number 4: "All Special Units formed during the war period on the territories of the Security Services Centres are to be immediately disassembled and put at the disposal of the army of the Serbian Republic ..." So they're not to be arrested, they're not to be prosecuted, they're to be put at the disposal of the army of the Serbian Republic. And that was echoed in a later order that we'll see in a moment. Apart from issuing written orders, Mico Stanisic held regular meetings, as he himself said, with his CSB chiefs and other high-ranking members of the RS MUP. On July the 11th in, in fact, Belgrade, although it says -- the brief analysis is headed Sarajevo, the meeting took place in Belgrade. And if we just look at the first page and you'll see it says at the top this was a meeting held in Belgrade. And if we look at the people who were there, it's virtually the same that we saw in the 11th of February meeting, as I say, all of who by this stage got high positions and with others. But we see Stanisic, Kljajic, and we see what positions they received there. Slobodan Skipina, Under-Secretary of State Security Service. Assistant ministers Vlasko Kusmuk, Planojevic, Njegus -- go down a bit further -- see some of the names. If we go down to the middle we see Stojan Zupljanin. You see there Goran -- yeah, from here. A bit further up. Jusurovic [sic], Goran Radovic, Stojan Zupljanin, Nedeljko Kesic, and so on and so forth. It's a very long document and we'll look at it when we reach that evidence. In fact, he also sent a report of that meeting, this is just to show the communication and cooperation between the -- him and other people involved in this enterprise. He sent a report on the 17th of July to Radovan Karadzic. You'll see -- no, can we just go -- sorry, I just want to go to the front page. Can we move a bit -- yeah. President of the -- to the president of the Presidency, who was Radovan Karadzic, and the prime minister. Report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead. It was in fact a report of July and [indiscernible] so it's a long report. He also sent out, even during the course of the conflict, inspectors to the various CSBs and SJBs. In June he received a report on Brcko, Zvornik, and Bijeljina. And in August he was sent a full report on the activities of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik. And if we look, first of all, at April -- there's an earlier one. It's not working at the moment. 17th of June, that's an earlier one -- although -- sorry, can we just go back to that for the moment. I beg your pardon. This is an earlier one. But it's actually quite interesting because it's 21st of April, so -- but it says under Zvornik -- Zvornik really was one of the worst municipalities for violence and the like. "... the town is under Serbian militia reserve and the -- and reserve TO. The town is being cleaned ..." This is 21st of April. And the 17th of June -- yeah. This is the -- a report on the inspection, what was found at Brcko, Zvornik, and partially at Bijeljina. Now, if we go to the second page, this is purely on the basis of his knowledge: "Considering that a large number of crimes were also committed by members of the Brcko Public Security Station, it was agreed that they should continue gathering intelligence and other information ..." Next page, middle paragraph, a lot of information about Captain Dragan and Goran Jelisic and if we get to the bottom, certain Goran Jelisic -- why are we suddenly going to blue? "Goran Jelisic had committed crimes of rape and murder of innocent Muslims. The same as bragging around Brcko and Bijeljina about his evil doings. The police employees in direct contact with him are in fear of him pulling a weapon at them because he is, as they say, unpredictable, and it is enough for a policeman to look at him the wrong way for a conflict to break out."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I just have one intervention in the transcript. It's page 60, line 15, I believe the document says and my colleague says "certain Goran Jelisic committed rape and murder of innocent Muslims." Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I said "certain." If one looks a bit more on this report -- all right, let's not bother. We'll deal with this report when we come to the evidence. Just -- it's that document. This is the 4th of August, 1992. "We are hereby submitting as an attachment a report on the activities of the MUP to detect the criminal activities of the Yellow Wasps ..." And then the next document is the actual report. As I say, it was only at the end of July and effectively it was because the Yellow Wasps had attacked a car. It's not altogether at the moment clear from the evidence whether it was a car that Stanisic himself was in or Velibor Ostojic and that then brought the wrath of the authorities down on this particular group. So that is a, as it were, a quick look at the -- some of the -- I mean only some of the evidence that shows Mico Stanisic's knowledge and involvement. As far as Stojan Zupljanin is concerned, we've already seen that he complied with the orders given to him by Mico Stanisic, but he was also ideologically committed to the goals of the Bosnian Serb SDS leadership from the early days. If you recall, yesterday we looked at the letter he wrote to Mrs. Plavsic complaining about the paper being changed to green. As we said, Banja Luka was Serb controlled, strategically important, and contained the headquarters of one of the biggest corps in the VRS. That enabled Stojan Zupljanin to liaise directly with General Talic in respect of joint operations. Moreover, he also had direct contact with Radovan Karadzic from 1991. That cannot be said of many of the chiefs of the CSBs. If we look at the screen this was 7th of August, 1991. Again, it's an intercept of a conversation between Karadzic and Zupljanin and in -- Karadzic says he -- when he comes in and he says Zupljanin here. He doesn't have to say, By the way, I'm Stojan Zupljanin, and I'm chief of the CSB, or whatever. It's straight Zupljanin here. Most of the conversation seems to concern some businessmen from Zagreb and some shady dealings, but at page 3: "I'm sending you my regards from Banja Luka," he says. "Keep on fighting and following your course." And Karadzic says: "Thank you very much. "So that you know in that these last moves and the tactics that you've been developing, I think they're extremely good and just keep on going." And then Karadzic says: "I hope the people will realise what's better for them so they can see for themselves." And then there's conversation about Alija Izetbegovic. And then over the page, Zupljanin, in the middle page, says: "What good that would do us, no way. Here, I've been listening to the news tonight, and Alija's trying some things but our guess is that, in a way, this is the beginning of his end." Karadzic said: "Yes, I believe he'll lose a lot among his people, and that hawk's nest of his. "Yes. "He wants to isolate himself," says Karadzic. At 10 per cent of Serbs holding entire Croatia by the throat over there, what could 35 per cent do here? Yes, absolutely, and fight along a peaceful course, for we really have no interest in that. In May, and I think we have looked at that, he gave instructions, we looked at some documents to the SJBs about the disarmament policy, there may be one more, dated the 14th of May, to the chiefs of all public security stations, et cetera, et cetera. "In keeping with the ... autonomous region of Bosnian Krajina regarding the surrender of illegally owned weapons ... public security stations must undertake the following ..." And he sets out what they have to do. And on the last part -- no, sorry -- "Measures." "Measures activities in the event of possible resistance particularly of the people against whom the planned activities are being taken." And then 6 and 7: "Plans for the seizure of illegally owned weapons, ammunition, and explosive devices must immediately be sent to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre for verification. "Reports on the results of the planned activities must be sent to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre ..." I think that this demonstrates yet again the -- as I say, the rigidly hierarchical and controlled nature of this particular force. In fact, the VRS were rather worried about what they -- the CSBs and SJBs intended to do. If you just look at a report for -- virtually I think it's the same -- the day after. We look at situation on the ground, the last few lines, "since," "since the dead-line ..." Yeah, in that paragraph. Thanks. "Since the dead-line for handing over illegally owned weapons has expired and the Banja Luka MUP organs are making appropriate preparations to take away the weapons, people fear possible interethnic conflicts." He forwarded orders he received from Mico Stanisic to the SJBs, and there's quite an interesting one here. Again, 15th of May, sent from the Banja Luka services centre to all SJBs, to the chief, and it says: "We received the communication ... from the Serbian Republic of the BH MUP ..." and this is to do with individual cases and people committing crimes. Last paragraph: "Employees who do not fulfill the conditions prescribed for police reserves are to return their equipment to the police stations and to be placed at the disposal of the Serbian Territorial Defence." As far as the Special Police are concerned, their behaviour, it's quite clear from the evidence we've looked at, particularly in Kotor Varos, that Stojan Zupljanin knew what they were doing. But on the 13th of June, even Prijedor police station, even Simo Drljaca was prompted to send a report to the chief of the security services about the special unit. With respect to the deployment of Banja Luka Security Services Special Unit, the following can be stated, and then there is a long paragraph about everything that they had done, arbitrarily arresting, interrogating, abusing the prisoners, stealing the jewellery, scandalised the police officers there, and so on and so forth. And then it says: "The help that we received from the Special Unit of the Banja Luka Security Services during the attack on Prijedor was valuable but after the joint action of the army, the Special Unit and our police, I received many complaints about the conduct of the Special Unit and their looting during mopping-up operations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on the -- this aspect of what Stojan Zupljanin was aware of, on the 20th of July he sent a report to the minister. And if one looks at the second paragraph, he deals with the army and police arresting a great number of citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality who were, depending on the number of and circumstances on the field sent to various buildings. "According to our information, this situation involves several thousands of mostly military-aged men. They were subject to operational procedures by military services, service for national and public security, which then carried out a selection ... three categories ... first and second ... security interest ... third category made up of adult men on which, so far, the security service doesn't have any information of security interest for us, so they can be treated as hostages." Finally, as far as the expulsion -- finally on this topic. As far as expulsion of non-Serbs were concerned, the evidence will show that the RS MUP was instrumental in the providing of buses to transport the non-Serbs guarding the buses and committing crimes and sometimes murder. I want to deal briefly with the failure to investigate or punish. As I've already really referred to throughout this opening, the evidence shows that neither Mico Stanisic nor Stojan Zupljanin did anything less really than pervert the function of a police force to protect lives and property of all persons who came within their jurisdiction. If they can't do that, the object of a police force is to investigate and punish the perpetrators of crimes, particularly those who commit the most serious crimes of murder, serious assaults, and unlawful detention. The Law on Internal Affair, Articles 12 and 15 made it quite clear that that was what they were supposed to be doing, as did the criminal procedure code. As we've seen, the criminal justice system continued to function during this period and the books that are part of this case from the Prosecutor's offices showed that arrests were being carried out and persons were being prosecuted. Paramilitary formations such as the Yellow Wasps who were committing these offences were actually being assisted by police. I'm not going to put the document up, but there is a document dated the 11th of July, which is up actually, which shows that they handed over weapons to Vojo Vuckovic, who was a member of the Yellow Wasps. And when orders were given for investigations of war crimes, this was always in respect of war crimes committed against Serbs. Very occasionally, when crimes against non-Serbs were so notorious that an investigation had to be launched, for some reason these investigations were unsuccessful, or if the persons were arrested, the judicial process was so stalled that no one was ever convicted. The Mount Vlasic killings that I've referred to were actually featured on an ABC Nightline programme, and Stojan Zupljanin was interviewed. And I think it might be worth just dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, one last question. The law that you referred to, the Law on Internal Affairs --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: -- was that an RS law or an old Yugoslav law or where -- who passed it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

What they didn't seem to manage to get to put together was a rule book so they used the old rule book, but the criminal procedure code applied throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF

And very recently, as you no doubt you have seen, there have been trials carrying on at the state court. So what one can say in brief conclusion, Your Honours, what was the end result of these crimes that were committed in 1992 in the municipalities which are reflected in this indictment? Exhumed bodies in these municipalities overall come to some 3.449. Of that, the scheduled incidents amount to 2.825. Some bodies, of course, have never been recovered. Missing overall in these municipalities 4.411 people. Displaced persons from these municipalities run into the hundreds of thousands. And so we end where effectively we began yesterday. We suggest that what happened, the pattern of events, can only have come about as a result of a preconceived plan, a joint enterprise, devised and put into execution by those at all levels of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And we are confident that when you've heard all the evidence in this case you will be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the two accused knowingly and fully participated in the criminal enterprise which we allege.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We were discussing yesterday the issue that had become clear to us just recently, namely, about the relevance of the report prepared -- the late -- the supplemental report prepared by Dr. Donia on the Siege of Sarajevo. And so we wanted you to point out to us which parts exactly of that report are of any relevance to this case and which of the documents that were coming in the wake of this document were actually linked to the document itself. So let's begin by those two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I start, first of all, Your Honours, with the relevance. It is perhaps a slightly misleading title in the sense that it says, The Bosnian Serb leadership and the Siege of Sarajevo, and it's different from the report that I know Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, is familiar with through having sat on the trial of Dragomir Milosevic. There are three Sarajevo municipalities in this indictment, that is to say Pale, Ilijas, and Vogosca. The report deals with the take-overs in all three, and I'll come to the various parts of the report in a moment, but can I just generally summarise why we say this is important and relevant. This report is a microcosm of the background to the take-overs in these municipalities. It will have the effect, if Your Honours allow it to go in, of stream-lining matters down the road and the effect of dealing with one of the aspects which I know is of concern to Your Honours, namely, that the trial should not last any longer than it must have to. If we do not have this report admitted and the various documents, it will require us to lead further evidence about the take-overs in this municipality to show the pattern of events which I've been referring to throughout my opening. The second matter is this: This report was only completed in -- well, end of May/June this year, which is why it was disclosed at a later stage. It was actually disclosed in June to the Defence and given to Your Honours in August. Therefore, Dr. Donia had the opportunity to look at material which wasn't available to him when he did his earlier reports for Krajisnik, for the Brdjanin case, for the Dragomir Milosevic, including a great deal of intercept evidence which only came to light shortly before he did this report. And he is, therefore, able to deal with that. In addition to that, he has referred to a great deal of open-source material such as books and newspaper articles which would not otherwise be before this Court. So having said all that, can I take Your Honours through the report and show you why we say it is relevant. Leaving aside the introduction which merely sets out his methodology, he then deals with Sarajevo and the multi-party elections of 1990. Your Honour asked me yesterday about where these municipalities were and the like, and he deals with exactly all of that in that particular paragraph -- chapter, which is chapter 2. He explains particularly the multicultural, multinational make-up of Sarajevo which is important because we say it's one of the reasons why you couldn't say this is going to be Serb territory. He then deals in chapter 3 with regionalisation in general. He's already dealt with that in some other reports and Variant A & B. So to that extent, I agree. That was just probably a repetition of his earlier reports. I don't believe there's anything except that he talks about the SAO Romanija Birac at page 16. Perhaps you might look at that if Your Honours be kind enough. From its inception, the SAO Romanija Birac was to be the Bosnian Serb counterpart to the city government of Sarajevo. So he explains that. Then he deals with Variant A & B. And then can I come -- this is the meat, I suppose. Chapter 4, the SDS political take-over of Sarajevo's suburbs and the three municipalities we're dealing with, I suppose, would count for Sarajevo's suburbs. He talks about Jovan Tintor at page 23, who figures in this case that you're going to hear, and then at page 24 we get directly to one of the municipalities that we're actually dealing with in this case, Pale. And you will see in that paragraph, page 24, SDS leaders and then an interview with police chief or with Malko Koroman, who you've heard about in the opening, who's going to again figure largely. And he has dealt with an article, which otherwise -- if I have -- if we have to try and get this all in and you've already told us some months ago, I think it was, that the report would go in as a document with the -- that we didn't have to separately list all the footnotes on our 65 ter list. And here he's quoting Malko Koroman from an interview in something -- in a magazine called Policajac and deals with what happened. And if we go through, there's a lot about Koroman, and it's all about Pale until page 27, where we deal with Ilijas, also one of our municipalities. And again, because he's got the opportunity and because he's a professional historian, he has looked at sources and material, all of which he's listed which otherwise to get in before you as evidence would require us to double virtually the number of exhibits. He goes on to deal with other municipalities just to give the general picture. And may I say, we will be concentrating on the ones that are particularly relevant to our case or mention the MUP. This is what the case is about. If you go to page 38, "Other Municipalities," second paragraph, under that head, he talks about Vogosca, which is the third of the three Sarajevo municipalities that this case is concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. In my page 38 I -- in the second paragraph under "Other Municipalities," --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: SDS --

Your Honours, chapter 5 deals with the military preparations, but in general, not specifically, in Sarajevo. It's how the formation of the VRS and the like came about. That again sets out the background. Again, some of it is dealt with in his earlier reports. Some he's able to produce new -- a new light from new documents. If you go to page 50, the second paragraph deals with the barricades incident, which I've already talked about in opening, which is clearly part of our case because of the involvement of so many of the RS MUP in it. utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I can concur with Your Honour and Ms. Korner that it was actually at that -- on that particular meeting that we discussed this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, a Senior Legal Officer was present as well and I believe a transcript has been asked for but we haven't had one yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's not waste any more time on this issue. The heart of the matter is that the Chamber is disturbed by the fact that you only come here only a couple of days before Donia actually appears and asks to have these 29 documents admitted into evidence, because we think that you should actually have known and seen and determined a long time ago that you would wish to use these 29 documents during the examination-in-chief of Dr. Donia. So why on earth are you coming with it in the last minute? It puts the Chamber into difficulty and it certainly puts the Defence into difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the problems we've had is that until we appeared here -- whenever the Pre-Trial Conference was, we didn't know what sort of time we were being given to call evidence. You may recall that we filed a motion applying that under the ruling made by Lord Bonomy, I believe it was, the experts were not under 94 but would come under a form of 92 bis or whatever. And I think at the Pre-Trial Conference, I think, Your Honour ruled that you just wanted them under Rule 94. And I see there's some nodding going on. Until that stage we didn't know and that's why we didn't produce the list, we didn't know how long we were going to get for Dr. Donia, how his evidence was going in. Now, I absolutely appreciate that we've had a week, more than a week, I'm not sure, as I say, I can't remember when the Pre-Trial Conference was, and that we should have done it than we did it, yes, but we simply got buried in motions and that's, I'm afraid, the only explanation. And all I can say is I'm sorry, but as Your Honours have ruled in any event that cross-examination on the Sarajevo report will not have to take place until later, the other documents are all ones which I have no doubt at all both my learned friends are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We would see things slightly differently, because if I recall your indications of the time that you would need to examine Dr. Donia, at no point did you indicate that you wanted to have more than three hours. Maybe there was one very early submission from your side where he was on for perhaps four hours, but I'm not sure of this. But it was either three or four hours, and so I think you could have and should have indeed made up your mind much earlier about the documents that you really wished to confront Mr. Donia with when he appears. And you could have done so knowing yourself that you wouldn't spend more than three or maybe four hours with him in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that would have been put you easily in a position where you could have made up your mind as to which documents would you wish to use, and so as to notify the Defence and ultimately the Chamber about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept the criticism. There's nothing else I can say but that we've selected these documents because we hoped that they would assist the Trial Chamber. The fact that for whatever reasons - and Your Honours say that's -- my explanation is not sufficient - and so I accept the criticism. All I can say is that we would like -- we've been warned by Your Honours about what will happen if we are late. I would like to say it will never happen again, but we will make -- that would possibly be too optimistic, but we will make every effort we can to make sure it doesn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What we will do now is that we will adjourn for 10 or maybe 15 minutes and deliberate on the matter, and we'll be back here in court at quarter to 7.00 and hand down our ruling on these two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have only three and a half minutes left and I don't want to pull the same stunt as we did yesterday, so I'll try to offload the decisions that we have reached in the break. Thank you for waiting. Mrs. Korner, we are of the opinion that only parts of the Donia report are of relevance to this case, and we will therefore identify chapters 4, 5, and what should have been 6 as the parts of the report which we will admit. This means that for your examination-in-chief in relation to this report you will limit yourselves to questions relating to chapter 4, 5, and what should have been 6. And to be clear, I better line out the page numbers. It's from page 23 to and including page 54. So 30 pages out of the report we will allow, and the rest is out. In relation to the documents, the 29 documents, included in your motion of I think it was 14th of August, it follows from the first decision that out of those 29 documents which you have moved to have included, we will allow you to admit those documents that are mentioned in the footnotes of those three chapters. I can't on top of my head tell you which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I suppose that a small number of the 29 documents are mentioned in the footnotes of those three chapters, and those we will allow you to include in your 65 ter list. The remaining documents in that group of 29 cannot be introduced into your witness -- into your exhibit list, 65 ter list, at least not through this witness. And finally, I think I have one minute more, regarding the time for Donia tomorrow. It turns out - and we have received this information from the Registry - that Popovic is actually cancelled for tomorrow. So we could begin earlier on in order to make sure that there is enough time for you to complete your examination-in-chief minus the three chapters and for the Defence teams to conclude their cross-examination on the Donia reports except the three chapters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. No, no. Let me just -- what we propose, and we have 45 seconds left, is that if you wish to begin at 12.15, the Chamber and the Defence team hopefully will remain available to you; otherwise, we begin at 2.15, as scheduled. But if by the end of your proofing with Dr. Donia tomorrow and if you're nervous about the time, then you can pick up the phone and let us know if you wish to begin at 12.15 because that will add another 90 minutes to the time that you have available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful. Can I very quickly -- we'll certainly do that. The only difficulty we foresee is that we've got to work out and extract the documents. And the other matter in the ten seconds left, do Your Honours -- would Your Honours like hard copy binders of the documents that he's going to refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't know about my colleagues. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- I take it from the internet or the e-court system. But my colleagues, would you like to have hard copies provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I will try to make do without hard copies for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Could you let us know which of the 29 documents appear in those three -- in the footnotes of those three chapters sometime tomorrow before Dr. Donia comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can. We will e-mail all parties so that everybody knows. Sorry, one last -- please, one last thing. Would Your Honours make an order formally, which I understand you have to, that the court will sit on Thursday morning rather than Thursday afternoon. We're still appearing on the court list as Thursday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That order is hereby made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And one final question. When should -- perhaps we can discuss it tomorrow, but I would like to ask the Defence then to consider how long time do they need to prepare for the cross-examination of the three chapters? You don't have to answer now, but by tomorrow because otherwise we'll spend more time. But please have an answer ready for us by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This meeting is adjourned. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
